lessons.title: Why and how pollination is controlled
lessons.html:
Why and how pollination is controlled

Plant breeders make new cultivars by crossing chosen parents, and they keep breeding lines pure by self-pollinating them. In both cases, the breeder must know exactly which pollen fertilised which flower. Controlled pollination means stopping unwanted pollen from reaching the female flower and placing the chosen pollen on it by hand.

Basic flower biology

  • Pollen is produced by the male parts of the flower (anthers).
  • It must land on the female part (stigma, or the silks in maize) to fertilise the ovule and form a seed.
  • Some crops, like maize and sunflower, are mainly cross-pollinated by wind or insects. Others, like wheat, soybeans and dry beans, mostly self-pollinate inside the flower.

Types of controlled pollination

TypeMeaning
Self-pollination (selfing)Pollen from the same plant is placed on its own female flower
Sib-pollinationPollen from a plant of the same line or family
Cross-pollination (crossing)Pollen from a different, chosen parent

Preparation

  • Study the crossing plan: which female rows are crossed with which male rows, how many pollinations are needed and the codes for each cross.
  • Prepare materials: shoot bags and tassel bags (for maize), glassine or paper bags, staplers, labels, permanent markers, forceps, alcohol for cleaning tools, and recording sheets or a tablet.
  • Monitor the nursery daily as flowering approaches, so that flowers are covered before they open or silks emerge.

Timing is everything. If even one stray pollen grain reaches the stigma before it is covered, the seed is not what the label says.

lessons.title: Carrying out hand pollination
lessons.html:
Carrying out hand pollination

The method differs by crop. Maize is a good example of a crop with separate male (tassel) and female (ear) flowers on the same plant.

Maize hand pollination

  1. Shoot bagging: before silks appear, cover the young ear shoot with a shoot bag. Cut back the husk tip if needed, as the protocol says.
  2. Silk cutting: when silks have emerged under the bag, they may be cut back so that a fresh, even brush of silks is ready for pollination.
  3. Tassel bagging: the day before pollinating, cover the tassel of the pollen parent with a tassel bag and fold it closed around the stem, to collect fresh, pure pollen.
  4. Pollinating: the next morning, when pollen is shedding, bend the tassel and shake pollen into the tassel bag. Quickly remove the shoot bag, pour pollen onto the silks and immediately cover the ear with the tassel bag. Staple it around the stalk.
  5. Labelling: write the cross or self code, date and your initials on the bag.

Crops with perfect flowers

For crops such as wheat or beans that have male and female parts in the same flower, the female parent must be emasculated: the anthers are removed with fine forceps before they shed pollen. The flower is then covered, and later chosen pollen is applied. This needs care and good eyesight; a magnifier helps.

Avoiding contamination

  • Clean hands and forceps with alcohol between different pollen sources.
  • Work in still conditions where possible. Wind spreads pollen.
  • Never reuse a tassel bag for a different pollen source.
  • If a bag is torn or blown off, record the pollination as contaminated.

Safety

Work in the early morning to avoid heat. Wear a hat and long sleeves; maize leaves cut skin. Drink water often. Watch for bees and snakes in the nursery.

lessons.title: Recording and harvesting pollinations
lessons.html:
Recording and harvesting pollinations

A pollination is only useful if it is correctly recorded. The breeder will use the seed for years, and every seed packet must be traceable to its parents.

Recording

  • Record each pollination on the nursery sheet or tablet: female row and plant, male row and plant, type (self, sib or cross), date and pollinator.
  • Use the same codes on the bag and in the record.
  • Record failed or doubtful pollinations, such as torn bags, silks already exposed or no pollen.
  • Count pollinations completed against the target in the crossing plan and report progress to the breeder daily.

Aftercare

Check bags after rain and wind. Replace damaged bags only if the protocol allows, and note it. Keep the nursery weeded and watered so that pollinated plants develop well. Protect the nursery from birds, monkeys and other animals.

Harvesting

  1. When the seed is mature, harvest each pollinated ear or pod with its bag or label.
  2. Keep each harvest separate in a labelled bag or envelope.
  3. Dry the seed to the right moisture for storage.
  4. Shell or thresh each one separately, cleaning equipment between them.
  5. Record the amount of seed from each pollination and store it in the germplasm store with its code.

Quality checks

Breeders may check purity of crosses later, for example by growing out plants or by laboratory markers. If a cross shows contamination, the record helps trace what went wrong.

Key points

  • Controlled pollination keeps parents known for breeding and pure lines.
  • Cover female flowers before they can receive stray pollen.
  • Collect fresh, pure pollen with tassel bags or from chosen flowers.
  • Emasculate perfect flowers before their anthers shed pollen.
  • Label bags and records with the same codes and record failures too.
